title: Measuring body temperature of freely moving mice under optogenetics-induced hypothermia
author: Takahashi, Sakurai, et al.
materials:
Timing: 1 day

steps.title: Prepare AAV vectors
steps.instruction: Obtain the Cre‑dependent OPN4dC‑mCherry construct (pAAV‑EF1a‑DIO‑hOPN4dC‑mCherry) and thaw the virus stock on ice; aliquot 3–4 µL portions, store each at –80 °C, and avoid repeated freeze‑thaw cycles.

steps.title: Prepare Qrfp‑iCre mice
steps.instruction: Use heterozygous Qrfp‑iCre mice (strain B6J.B6N‑Qrfp, RBRC11137); select age and sex appropriate for the experiment.

steps.title: Set up stereotaxic injection system
steps.instruction: Assemble a mouse stereotaxic apparatus with an isoflurane anesthesia machine, a micro‑syringe pump, and stereotaxic holders for syringes and optic fibers; include a skull drill, heat pad, and stereo microscope as shown in Figure 1.

steps.title: Sterilize surgical instruments
steps.instruction: Prepare 70 % ethanol, sterilized saline, sterilized scissors, tweezers, a Hamilton syringe (10 µL) with 33‑gauge needle, a 0.5 mm cranial drill bit, optic fiber tips (200 µm diameter, 0.5 NA, 6 mm length), dental cement with curing light, a heat pad, and a stereoscopic microscope.

steps.title: Prepare TA‑F10 transmitters
steps.instruction: Obtain TA‑F10 transmitters (Data Sciences International) for core body temperature (TB) and locomotor activity; note they are reusable unless the internal battery is exhausted, must be turned off after use, and are not rechargeable.

steps.title: Clean and sterilize TA‑F10
steps.instruction: After experiments, retrieve the transmitter from the abdominal cavity before perfusion, keep it in water, rinse off blood with running water, then soak sequentially: (a) 10 % Haemo‑Sol (water‑diluted) ≥ 4 h (ideally > 10 h); (b) 2 % glutaraldehyde (water‑diluted) ≥ 4 h (ideally > 10 h); (c) sterile saline ≥ 4 h to remove glutaraldehyde. Store in saline ≤ 48 h before implantation or dry and keep at 20–24 °C for long‑term storage.

steps.title: Prepare surgical tools for implantation
steps.instruction: Gather 70 % ethanol, sterile saline, scissors, tweezers, forceps, sterile suture needle and suture, a small‑animal isoflurane anesthesia machine, and a heat pad.

steps.title: Assemble telemetry recording platform
steps.instruction: Set up a thermostatic chamber (e.g., HC‑100, SHIN‑FACTORY) with an air circulator; place the PONEMAH receiver board inside, connect it to Matrix 2.0 (MX2) via LAN cable, attach a magnet and radio, and link to a computer running PONEMAH Physiology Platform v.6.30. Position a thermal camera ~80 cm above the cage for superficial temperature, and ensure a long patch cord and ample space above the cage for long‑term recordings. Verify laser intensity at the fiber tip is 10 µW for OPN4dC stimulation.

steps.title: Assemble infrared thermography platform
steps.instruction: Install an InfReC R550EX thermal imaging camera (or equivalent) with its analysis software (InfReC Analyzer NS9500 Professional) on a computer; use the same thermal chamber as above, and provide a hair clipper and hair‑removal cream for mouse preparation.

steps.title: Set up optogenetic stimulation hardware
steps.instruction: Connect fiber‑optic rotary joints for free‑moving mice to mono‑fiber patch cords (1 m long); use an optic laser emitting 460–480 nm light, adjustable to 10 µW at the fiber tip, and a pulse generator. Adjust patch‑cord length to match the distance between cage and rotary joint to avoid damage and allow unrestricted movement.

steps.title: Record body temperature during stimulation
steps.instruction: Choose either (a) implanted TA‑F10 transmitters to log core body temperature (TB) via the telemetry platform, or (b) the infrared camera to capture surface temperature over brown adipose tissue (TBAT) and tail; run the recording software while delivering optogenetic light pulses as programmed.

description: We have previously reported a hibernation-like state induced by the chemogenetic activation of Quiescence-inducing neurons (Q neurons) in mice.2 Q neurons are localized in the anteroventral periventricular nucleus (AVPe) of the hypothalamus and are molecularly defined by the expression of the neuropeptide pyroglutamylated RFamide peptide (QRFP). The Q-neuron-induced hypothermic and hypometabolic state (QIH) is similar to the hibernation observed in hibernators, such as ground squirrels and Syrian hamsters. We recently developed an optogenetic tool using a blue-light photoreceptor, human Opsin4 (OPN4), to generate a long-lasting QIH with a higher temporal resolution than the chemogenetics, a stimulatory hM3Dq designer receptor exclusively activated by the designer drug (DREADD) system.1 Modified OPN4 (OPN4dC) lacking the C-terminal region can be activated by weak light stimulation, allowing for prolonged manipulation of Q neurons (at least 24 h) without any brain damage. Here, we describe the materials and methods used for optogenetically inducing QIH and monitoring the body temperature of freely-moving mice. This technique will be useful in understanding the neuronal and molecular mechanisms of thermoregulation and hibernation. Additionally, OPN4dC optogenetics, which activates Gq signaling, can be used to manipulate other types of neurons and non-neuronal cells.1 Several studies have reported the induction of hypothermia in mice by neuronal manipulation and the measurement of body temperature during the process. However, the duration of optogenetic manipulation in these studies was limited to a few hours (Table 1). On the other hand, chemogenetics has been mainly used to induce hypothermia for a longer period (beyond a day),3,4,5 where the endpoint of stimulation is unclear owing to the gradual disappearance of the drug effect.
